epristeride.summary: An oral DHT-lowering drug of the finasteride family, sold in China for prostate enlargement and discussed by hair-loss communities for keeping scalp hair.

quick.overview:
Epristeride is an oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that people in hair-loss communities discuss as a finasteride-like way to hold on to scalp hair. It is sold in China for enlarged prostate.

It blocks the type 2 form of the enzyme that turns testosterone into DHT, the hormone linked to follicle miniaturisation and pattern hair loss. Less DHT means less thinning over time. Hair loss and acne were explored as uses during development but were never approved, and no published hair-loss trial results turned up.
quick.how: People who use it treat it as an alternative to finasteride, taken by mouth as a daily tablet, usually alongside other hair-loss measures. Hair-loss drugs of this type are generally kept up long term, with results judged over many months.
quick.risks: Safety information is sparse. As a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor it is prescription-only where it is marketed, and it is not sold in the US, UK or Japan.

angle.text: Epristeride lowers DHT, the hormone that shrinks scalp follicles, so the goal is slower thinning and more hair kept. Hair-loss forum users discuss it as a finasteride-like option. It is marketed in China for prostate enlargement, and its hair use was explored but never approved.

alfatradiol-ell-cranell-alpha.summary: A weak topical estrogen applied to the scalp, sold in Germany and Latin America to slow pattern hair loss in men and women.

quick.overview:
Alfatradiol is a topical form of 17-alpha-estradiol, applied to the scalp to slow pattern hair loss in men and women. It is sold in Germany and parts of Latin America, and users see it as a non-finasteride option.

It is described as blocking 5-alpha-reductase locally, lowering DHT in the scalp, and has weak estrogen-receptor activity. Reports describe it as slowing or stabilising loss rather than adding density. In a randomized comparison in 103 women, 2% minoxidil outperformed it.
quick.how: It is used as a liquid applied to the scalp, regularly and over the long term. People tend to use it alone or as a gentler alternative to minoxidil or oral DHT blockers.
quick.risks: Reported effects are mostly local itching or burning, attributed to the alcohol vehicle. Safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding and under 18 is unknown. It is not FDA approved.

angle.text: Alfatradiol is a scalp-applied weak estrogen that reduces local DHT activity, so follicles thin more slowly and more density is kept. Users apply it as a non-finasteride option for pattern hair loss in men and women. Trials describe slowed loss with little regrowth.

topilutamide-fluridil.summary: A scalp-applied antiandrogen sold in the Czech Republic and Slovakia to slow pattern hair loss without oral DHT blockers.

quick.overview:
Topilutamide (fluridil) is a scalp-applied antiandrogen sold as Eucapil in the Czech Republic and Slovakia for pattern hair loss in men and women. People interested in topical alternatives to oral DHT blockers discuss it.

It blocks the androgen receptor in the scalp, so follicles are less affected by DHT and thin more slowly. It is reported to break down quickly in human serum. Published data consists of small older studies and lab work; no large randomized trials were found.
quick.how: It is used as a 2% lotion applied to the scalp, regularly over months. Users often pair it with other hair-loss measures.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited. It is not approved by the FDA or EMA for hair loss.

angle.text: Topilutamide blocks androgen receptors at the scalp, so follicles shrink less under DHT and thinning slows. Users interested in topical options instead of oral DHT blockers discuss it. It is sold in two European countries, and published trial data is small.

dimethylcurcumin-asc-j9.summary: An experimental curcumin-derived anti-androgen cream that breaks down the androgen receptor, aimed at acne and tested in two Phase 2 trials.

quick.overview:
ASC-J9 (dimethylcurcumin) is an experimental curcumin-derived compound that has drawn interest as a topical acne approach. Instead of just blocking the androgen receptor, it lowers the amount of receptor protein in cells.

The idea is less androgen-driven oil and inflammation in skin, and so fewer breakouts. Two Phase 2 acne trials of a cream (2007 and 2011, around 180 participants each) are registered as completed, but no published results were found. Most other work is laboratory and animal research on conditions such as prostate cancer.
quick.how: It has been tested as a topical cream in clinical trials and is not available as an approved product, so there is no established routine for using it.
quick.risks: It is experimental and not approved by regulators. Human safety data from the acne trials are not published in the sources reviewed; most other data come from cell and animal studies.

angle.text: ASC-J9 aims at acne by reducing androgen receptor protein in skin, which should mean less oil and inflammation and fewer breakouts. It reached two Phase 2 acne cream trials, but no results were found.

drospirenone.summary: A progestin with anti-androgen action in some contraceptive pills, FDA-labelled for moderate acne in women who also want birth control.

quick.overview:
Drospirenone is a prescription progestin in some contraceptive pills. In the pill Yaz it is labelled in the US for moderate acne in women at least 14 who also choose the pill for contraception. Women use these pills for clearer skin, and the fluid retention seen with some older progestins is reduced.

It blocks androgen and mineralocorticoid receptors as well as activating the progesterone receptor, which lowers androgen signalling in skin and so oil production. Its antiandrogenic action is the usual explanation for the acne benefit.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth, most often as a combined pill with an estrogen on a daily schedule set by a prescriber. Skin changes with hormonal pills are generally judged over a few months.
quick.risks: Common effects include headache, irregular bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness and mood changes. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35, and registry studies have reported more venous clots with drospirenone pills than with levonorgestrel pills, though the size of the difference is debated. Rarely it can raise potassium. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Drospirenone blocks androgen receptors, which reduces sebum production and leads to clearer skin. It is prescribed to women in contraceptive pills, and the FDA labels certain drospirenone pills for moderate acne in women who also want contraception.

dienogest.summary: An antiandrogenic progestin in some contraceptive pills that women are prescribed partly for acne, and used alone for endometriosis.

quick.overview:
Dienogest is a prescription progestin, best known as a standalone endometriosis treatment and as the progestin in several combined pills. Because it is antiandrogenic, some ethinylestradiol/dienogest pills are used or labelled for acne in women who also want contraception.

It activates the progesterone receptor and blocks the androgen receptor, suppressing ovulation and reducing androgen effects such as oiliness and acne, without androgenic activity of its own. No acne-specific trials were found in the sources reviewed; its research base is mainly in endometriosis.
quick.how: For acne it is taken as a combined daily pill chosen by a prescriber, with availability and labelling that vary by country. Skin changes are generally judged over a few months.
quick.risks: Reported effects include irregular bleeding, headache, nausea, breast tenderness, mood changes and weight gain. Combined pills carry a boxed warning for smokers over 35 and an increased clot risk; long-term use may lower bone density. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Dienogest is an anti-androgenic progestin, so it eases oil gland stimulation and women on pills containing it get clearer skin. It is prescribed partly for acne through combined contraceptive pills. No acne-specific trials were found.

chlormadinone-acetate.summary: An antiandrogenic progestin in some European contraceptive pills prescribed to women for acne and oily skin.

quick.overview:
Chlormadinone acetate is a prescription progestin with antiandrogenic effects, found mainly in combined contraceptive pills such as Belara sold outside the US. Doctors use these pills for women with acne, oily skin or excess hair who also want contraception.

It blocks the androgen receptor and suppresses LH and FSH, lowering androgen effects in skin and hair follicles, so there is less sebum and clearer skin. Acne evidence comes from open-label studies, including one of an ethinylestradiol/CMA pill over 12 cycles; no large randomized acne trial was found.
quick.how: It is taken as a combined daily pill chosen by a prescriber, and benefits on skin are generally judged over several months of cycles.
quick.risks: Low-dose pills commonly cause irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. High doses have been linked to adrenal and metabolic effects, and prolonged high-dose use to meningioma. It is prescription-only and was withdrawn in the US around 1970 after dog mammary tumour findings.

angle.text: Chlormadinone acetate blocks the androgen receptor, so skin makes less sebum and breakouts and oiliness ease. Women use pills containing it for acne and oily skin. Support comes from open-label studies.

nomegestrol-acetate.summary: A mildly antiandrogenic progestin in European contraceptive pills, linked by its pharmacology to calmer, less oily skin.

quick.overview:
Nomegestrol acetate is a prescription progestin used with estradiol in the Zoely contraceptive pill and alone for some gynaecological conditions. It is sold in Europe and Australia but not the US. Some discussion links it to skin benefits for acne-prone users.

It has mild antiandrogenic activity, which could mean slightly less sebum and clearer skin, and reference works suggest it may help acne and oily skin. That link comes from its pharmacology; no acne trials were found.
quick.how: It is taken as a daily pill prescribed by a doctor, mainly as a contraceptive, and any skin effect is a side benefit seen over several months.
quick.risks: Reported effects are typically mild: irregular bleeding, headache, nausea and breast tenderness. Prolonged use at therapeutic doses has been associated with meningioma in epidemiological studies. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Nomegestrol acetate has mild anti-androgenic activity, which could mean slightly less sebum and clearer skin for acne-prone users of the pill. That link is inferred from its pharmacology, and no acne trial was found.

abiraterone-acetate.summary: A prescription prostate-cancer drug that cuts androgen production, raised in anti-androgen discussion as a theoretical route to protecting scalp hair or skin.

quick.overview:
Abiraterone acetate is a prescription oral drug for advanced prostate cancer. It comes up in androgen-focused discussion as a theoretical route to protecting scalp hair or skin, because it sharply lowers testosterone and DHT.

It inhibits the enzyme CYP17A1 in the testes, adrenal glands and tumours, cutting production of testosterone and related androgens; it is given with prednisone to offset the resulting hormone imbalance. No study among the sources reviewed has tested it for hair loss, acne or other appearance outcomes.
quick.how: It is not used for appearance. It is taken by mouth with prednisone under oncology supervision for prostate cancer.
quick.risks: Labelled risks include high blood pressure, low potassium, fluid retention, adrenal insufficiency, liver toxicity and fetal harm. It is prescription-only and used under oncology supervision.

angle.text: Abiraterone lowers the body's androgen production, so in theory less DHT reaches the follicle and hair thins more slowly. It is a prostate-cancer drug, not used for appearance, and no hair or skin studies were found.

cimetidine.summary: An acid-reducing H2 blocker with weak antiandrogen action, occasionally tried for acne and excess hair in women.

quick.overview:
Cimetidine is an over-the-counter and prescription acid reducer with a weak antiandrogenic effect, so some women have tried it for acne or excess hair growth. The hoped-for result is less sebum, fewer pimples and less hirsutism.

At high doses it weakly blocks the androgen receptor and affects estrogen metabolism. Wikipedia reports the effect is too weak to help much with those conditions and that such use is not recommended. No acne or hirsutism trials appear in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: It is a stomach-acid medicine taken by mouth, and its use for skin or hair is an off-label idea rather than a routine treatment.
quick.risks: Side effects are usually mild, such as diarrhea, rash, dizziness and fatigue; rare gynecomastia or sexual dysfunction occur, mainly at high doses. It inhibits liver enzymes and interacts with many drugs including warfarin and theophylline.

angle.text: Cimetidine's weak antiandrogen activity is the basis for trying it against acne and excess hair in women, with slightly less sebum and body hair as the aim. References describe the effect as small, and it is an off-label use.

erythromycin-acne.summary: A prescription antibiotic solution labelled in the US for acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit bacterial resistance.

quick.overview:
Topical erythromycin 2% is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne vulgaris. It is used for fewer red pimples in mild-to-moderate acne and is a long-established option, introduced in 1952.

It binds the bacterial ribosome and stops protein synthesis, reducing acne-associated bacteria and the inflammation they drive. Reference sources describe it as typically combined with benzoyl peroxide.
quick.how: It is applied to the skin as a solution, usually alongside benzoyl peroxide, which limits the development of antibiotic resistance. It is used as a prescribed course rather than indefinitely.
quick.risks: Local dryness, peeling, itching and redness occur, and hives are rare. Labels warn of antibiotic-associated colitis. Reference sources note the pairing with benzoyl peroxide is to limit resistance.

angle.text: Topical erythromycin reduces acne bacteria, which lowers inflammation and leaves fewer red pimples. It is a prescription antibiotic labelled in the US for acne, and people typically pair it with benzoyl peroxide to limit bacterial resistance.

sulfacetamide.summary: A sulfa antibiotic, usually combined with sulfur in prescription lotions and washes for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.

quick.overview:
Sodium sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic applied to the skin, often combined with sulfur, in prescription lotions and washes for acne, rosacea with bumps and seborrheic dermatitis. People use it for clearer, less red skin.

It blocks bacterial folic acid synthesis to slow bacterial growth, and sulfur adds a keratolytic (skin-shedding) effect. Together they calm inflamed skin and reduce breakouts. The sources reviewed describe its role rather than citing trial results.
quick.how: It is used as a leave-on lotion or a wash on a routine set by a prescriber, often alongside other skin treatments.
quick.risks: Mild stinging, dryness and irritation are most common. The US label warns of Stevens-Johnson syndrome in sulfonamide-sensitive people and reports of drug-induced lupus, including one fatal case. People allergic to sulfa drugs should avoid it. Prescription product in the US.

angle.text: Sulfacetamide, usually combined with sulfur, works through antibacterial and skin-shedding action to calm inflamed skin, giving fewer breakouts and less redness. It is a prescription lotion or wash for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.

nadifloxacin.summary: A topical quinolone antibiotic cream for acne used in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia, but not approved in the US.

quick.overview:
Nadifloxacin is a 1% antibiotic cream for acne and skin infections, available in Japan and some European and Asian countries. People elsewhere discuss it as an import option for fewer pimples.

It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase, killing or stopping acne-related bacteria such as Cutibacterium acnes, and may have anti-inflammatory effects. Small studies reportedly show lesion reductions comparable to clindamycin combinations, though evidence in the sources is limited.
quick.how: It is applied to the skin as a cream over a prescribed course where it is sold.
quick.risks: Effects are mostly local burning, itching and dryness. Wikipedia notes concern that topical quinolones could promote resistance. Not approved in the US.

angle.text: Nadifloxacin is a topical antibiotic that kills acne bacteria and cuts inflammation, so fewer pimples form. It is used for acne in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia, and has been studied in clinical settings.

azithromycin-pulse-acne.summary: Short intermittent courses of an oral antibiotic prescribed off-label to calm inflamed acne for clearer skin.

quick.overview:
Azithromycin is a prescription macrolide antibiotic that some dermatologists prescribe in short, intermittent courses for inflammatory acne, often as an alternative to tetracycline-class antibiotics. The payoff is fewer inflamed lesions and clearer skin.

It blocks bacterial protein synthesis and builds up in tissues with a half-life of about 68 hours, which is why short or intermittent courses are used. The target in acne is Cutibacterium acnes. Published support is mostly small registered trials against doxycycline or minocycline, or with add-ons such as probiotics.
quick.how: It is taken by mouth on a few days each week on a schedule set by the prescriber, as an off-label option often used when other antibiotics are not suitable. Acne guidance generally recommends courses of no more than about three months.
quick.risks: Common effects are gastrointestinal. The FDA has warned about QT prolongation, and acne guidance cautions that repeated antibiotic exposure has increased resistant C. acnes. Prescription-only.

angle.text: Short azithromycin courses lower inflammation, so there are fewer inflamed lesions and clearer skin. Dermatologists sometimes prescribe them off-label for inflammatory acne, and the evidence consists of small head-to-head trials.

aminolevulinic-acid-photodynamic-therapy.summary: A clinic procedure pairing topical ALA with light, labelled for actinic keratoses and studied for acne and oilier skin.

quick.overview:
ALA photodynamic therapy applies aminolevulinic acid to the skin and then shines light on it. Its labelled uses are actinic keratosis and superficial basal cell carcinoma, and it is also investigated for acne and skin quality, where people hope for less oil and clearer skin.

The skin converts ALA into protoporphyrin IX, which light activates to produce reactive oxygen species that damage targeted cells, such as oil glands and bacteria. A 2016 systematic review called it safe and effective for acne, while one phase II trial found no advantage over blue/violet light alone.
quick.how: It is done in a clinic: the solution is applied, left to incubate, then the area is lit with a lamp, with eye protection. Treatments are repeated in a course set by the clinician.
quick.risks: Common effects are redness, pain or burning and a period of photosensitivity. The label also warns of hypersensitivity, transient amnestic episodes and eye injury from the lamp. Acne is not a labelled use.

angle.text: Light activates ALA in the skin, damaging oil glands and bacteria, with the hope of less acne and smoother skin. Clinics use it for actinic keratoses, and its acne use is investigational with mixed trial results.

trichloroacetic-acid-tca-peel.summary: A medium-depth chemical peel done by clinicians to renew skin, smoothing texture and fading pigment and some scars.

quick.overview:
TCA is a strong acid used as a medium-depth chemical peel. Clinicians use it for smoother texture, less uneven pigment and some acne scars, with visible skin renewal after healing.

The acid causes controlled chemical injury to the skin surface, which then peels and regenerates, and the depth depends on concentration and technique. Small trials are registered for acne, melasma, lentigines and scars, but the registry entries cited do not report results.
quick.how: It is a provider-performed procedure in a clinic or outpatient setting. A warm or burning sensation is common, and the skin peels over the following days before new skin shows.
quick.risks: The European Chemicals Agency says the acid causes severe skin burns and eye damage. Deeper peels carry risks of prolonged redness, pigment change, milia, atrophy and scarring, and Wikipedia says medium peels should be done by a medical provider.

angle.text: A TCA peel removes damaged outer skin so new skin forms in its place, leaving smoother texture and less pigment and scarring. Clinicians perform it, and the visible renewal shows after healing.

corticosteroid-injection-kenalog-for-cys.summary: A clinician-given steroid injection into a single inflamed pimple to shrink swelling and redness quickly.

quick.overview:
Intralesional steroid injection places a small amount of a corticosteroid such as triamcinolone (Kenalog) directly into an inflamed acne lesion. Acne communities discuss it as a way to shrink and calm one large cyst or nodule quickly.

Triamcinolone is a potent glucocorticoid that reduces inflammation where it is placed, so swelling drops, the lesion flattens and redness fades. It has documented dermatologic uses, including keloid and hypertrophic scars, but no acne-cyst trials appear in the sources used here.
quick.how: It is done by a clinician for individual lesions and is an off-label use. It is aimed at single pimples rather than overall acne.
quick.risks: It is prescription-only. Documented effects from other injection routes include raised eye pressure and, with intravitreal use, rare endophthalmitis; systemic effects such as menstrual irregularity are listed by Wikipedia.

angle.text: A steroid injected into a single inflamed pimple lowers swelling and inflammation, so the cyst flattens and redness fades. Acne forum users describe it as a clinician-given quick fix, and it is an off-label procedure.

basil-oil-acne.summary: A plant essential oil promoted as a natural topical for acne, with lab antibacterial activity against the acne bacterium.

quick.overview:
Basil oil is distilled from Ocimum basilicum and is rich in linalool and estragole. It is promoted in natural-skincare circles as a topical for fewer breakouts.

In the lab, constituents such as linalool and eugenol show antimicrobial activity, and one in vitro test of Thai basil oils targeted the acne bacterium. How this would translate to skin has not been studied in people, and no human acne trial was found.
quick.how: It is used in natural-skincare routines as a diluted topical, usually as part of a broader regimen.
quick.risks: No human safety data for acne use are cited. Essential oils can irritate or sensitize skin, and basil oil has shown cytotoxicity in cell-line studies.

angle.text: Basil oil is promoted as a topical whose antibacterial plant compounds reduce acne bacteria and breakouts. Lab tests, including against the acne bacterium, show antibacterial activity, and no human acne studies were found.

seaweed-oligosaccharides.summary: Brown-seaweed-derived sugars marketed as a complementary topical ingredient for acne-prone skin.

quick.overview:
Seaweed oligosaccharides are short sugar chains from brown seaweed such as Laminaria digitata, marketed as a topical ingredient for acne-prone skin, alone or as a zinc complex. The aim is a calmer, more balanced skin surface and fewer blemishes.

The main source is a 2013 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Science, which frames them as a marine-derived addition to benzoyl peroxide, antibiotics and retinoids as topical acne treatments. No further trial data were found, and detailed mechanisms are not given.
quick.how: They are used as a complementary topical ingredient in skincare, alongside standard acne products.
quick.risks: No safety data are cited, and effects on acne are not well characterized.

angle.text: Seaweed oligosaccharides are marine-derived sugars applied to acne-prone skin to calm the skin surface and reduce blemishes. They are marketed as a complementary ingredient, and the support is a single literature review.

bumetanide.summary: A potent prescription loop diuretic that appears in gray-market water-pill talk for a drier look; no study has tested it for facial puffiness.

quick.overview:
Bumetanide is a loop diuretic prescribed for swelling caused by heart, liver or kidney disease. It appears in gray-market water-pill talk among people aiming for a drier, sharper facial look through quick water-weight loss.

It blocks the NKCC2 sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter in the loop of Henle, so less sodium and water are reabsorbed and urine output rises. Effects begin within about an hour and last around six hours. No published study has examined it for facial depuffing or any appearance goal.
quick.how: It is a prescription medicine taken by mouth (a nasal-spray form also exists) for edema. Appearance use is informal, with people timing it for short-term water loss.
quick.risks: The US label carries a boxed warning that excessive amounts can cause profound water and electrolyte depletion and requires medical supervision. Reported effects include cramps, dizziness, low blood pressure, low potassium and, rarely, hearing loss and serious skin reactions. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Australia and is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency.

angle.text: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic that flushes water, so less fluid retention might leave a leaner, less puffy face. It appears in gray-market water-pill talk, but it is a prescription diuretic for edema and no study has tested it for facial puffiness.
